background.title: What a timed topic test is for
background.html:
A topic test checks one topic the way an exam does: a fixed time, no notes, marks printed in brackets after each question, for example [3]. Today the times come from the test covers: they are exam pace, a bit faster than normal homework.

The point is not the score. The point is to find out which exact points you cannot yet write down under time, so you can fix them before the exam.

background.title: How a mark scheme gives marks
background.html:
A mark scheme is the list of answers a marker accepts. For a written question it lists separate points, and each different correct point is worth one mark, up to the number in brackets. A scheme often lists more points than there are marks ("any two of these").

  • Say the same thing twice: still one mark.
  • Your words can differ from the scheme if the meaning is the same.
  • A vague word ("sticks" for adhesion) may not get the mark.

background.title: Command words: what the question wants
background.html:
The first word of a question tells you how much to write.

  • State: one word or short phrase.
  • Outline: the main points, briefly.
  • Describe: say what something is like or what happens.
  • Explain: say why or how, with "because" and "so".
  • Compare and contrast: what is the same and what is different.
  • Suggest: a sensible idea, even for something you were not taught.

background.title: SL and HL on one paper
background.html:
Biology is taught at standard level (SL) and higher level (HL). HL students learn everything SL students learn plus some extra parts ("additional higher level").

These InThinking tests are one paper for both levels: the HL-only questions come at the end, and the cover gives two times and two totals. You are HL, so you answer every question and use the HL time and total.

terms.def: The list of answers the marker accepts, with how many marks each point earns.
Done against a clock, with the time limit of the real exam, and no notes.
Higher level: the longer Biology course you take. HL exams have extra questions on the HL-only parts.
Standard level: the shorter Biology course. The tests show the SL time and total too, but you use the HL ones.
A question with answers A, B, C and D where you pick one. One mark each.
A question split into short parts, each worth a few marks.
A longer written answer, worth about 4 to 8 marks, where you make several separate points.
Writing down everything you remember about a topic on a blank page, from memory, before you look at anything.
Short revision notes for each topic (Revision Village, in your Drive), one or two pages long.
Matching so they fit together: in DNA, A always pairs with T and C with G.
A pattern used to make a copy. Each old DNA strand is the pattern for building a new strand.
One building block of DNA or RNA: a phosphate, a sugar and a base joined together.
A small group containing phosphorus and oxygen. It links the sugars in DNA and RNA into a chain.
In DNA and RNA, the part of a nucleotide that carries the code: A, C, G and T (U in RNA).
A strong bond where two atoms share a pair of electrons (tiny negative particles). It holds atoms together inside a molecule.
A weak attraction between a slightly positive hydrogen and a slightly negative atom such as oxygen. It holds the two DNA strands together and water molecules to each other.
The sugar in DNA. RNA has a very similar sugar called ribose.
A base found only in RNA. It takes the place of thymine (T).
A protein that DNA is wound around, like thread round a spool, so the long molecule fits in the nucleus.
The molecule that carries the instructions passed from parent to offspring. In living things it is DNA.
A single sugar unit, such as glucose.
Two sugar units joined together, such as sucrose (table sugar).
A long chain of many sugar units, such as starch or glycogen.
The energy store made of glucose chains in animals, kept in the liver and muscles.
Anything in an experiment that can change, such as temperature. You keep all but the one you test the same.
In an experiment, a set-up that leaves out the thing being tested (for example no yeast), to show that the result is caused by it.
Two carbon atoms joined by two shared pairs of electrons instead of one. Each one puts a bend in a fatty acid chain.
The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid. Fats with more bends melt at lower temperatures, so they are oils.
Having a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end, because electrons are shared unequally.
Symbols for slightly positive (δ+) and slightly negative (δ−). δ is the Greek letter delta.
Water sticking to other materials, such as soil or plant cell walls, by hydrogen bonds.
With no positive and negative ends. Non-polar substances such as oils do not mix with water.
The upward push of water that helps things float.
How much energy it takes to warm something up. Water needs a lot, so lakes and seas change temperature slowly.
How easily heat passes through a material. Water carries heat away from a body faster than air.
How thick and slow-flowing a liquid is. Honey has high viscosity; water much lower.
To turn from a gas into a liquid, as steam does on a cold window.
The distance from a star where a planet is not too hot and not too cold, so liquid water could exist.
IB command word: give the main points briefly.
IB command word: say why or how, with reasons (use "because" and "so").
IB command words: give what is the same (similarities) and what is different (differences), mentioning both things each time.
